title: Your Thymus May Decide How Long You Live, Two Major Studies Find
excerpt: Harvard-led research published in Nature reveals the long-overlooked chest gland strongly predicts longevity, cardiovascular risk, and cancer immunotherapy outcomes in adults.
body:
• Adults with a healthy thymus had a 50% lower risk of premature death and 63% lower cardiovascular mortality over 12 years, according to AI analysis of 27,000 CT scans.
  • Thymic health also predicted immunotherapy response in 3,400 cancer patients, outperforming standard tumor biomarkers.
  • Smoking, obesity, metabolic syndrome, and chronic inflammation were linked to faster thymic decline — suggesting the organ's deterioration may be partly preventable.
  • The findings, published in two Nature papers, challenge decades of medical orthodoxy that the thymus becomes irrelevant after puberty.

For generations, medical students learned a simple lesson about the thymus: the small, butterfly-shaped gland behind the breastbone trains T cells during childhood, then fades into irrelevance by puberty. Surgeons routinely cut it out during cardiac procedures because it sits in front of the heart.

That textbook narrative is now unravelling. Two studies published in the same issue of Nature in March 2026 — both led by Harvard Medical School researcher Hugo Aerts — present the strongest evidence yet that the thymus remains consequential throughout adult life, shaping how long people live and how effectively their bodies fight cancer.

An AI Deep Dive Into 27,000 Scans

Aerts and his team at Mass General Brigham's Artificial Intelligence in Medicine Program developed a machine-learning model that scores thymic health from routine chest CT scans. The system was trained on radiographs from 5,674 people and validated across more than 27,000 adults drawn from two major cohorts: the National Lung Screening Trial and the long-running Framingham Heart Study.

The model assigns each thymus a health tier — bottom 25%, middle 50%, or top 25%. Over a 12-year follow-up, adults in the top tier showed dramatically better outcomes than those in the bottom: a 50% lower risk of dying from any cause, a 63% lower risk of cardiovascular death, and a 36% lower risk of developing lung cancer.

""He called the results 'pretty amazing.'"

The Thymus Link to Lifestyle

The studies also identified modifiable factors tied to thymic health."

"The thymus has been overlooked for decades and may be a missing piece in explaining why people age differently, and why cancer treatments fail in some patients."

— Hugo Aerts, Professor, Harvard Medical School and Director of AI in Medicine at Mass General Brigham

"In some people, it stayed very active until a very old age," Aerts told Scientific American. "And in other people, it actually declined very rapidly at a younger age." That variation, the researchers found, carries real health consequences — even after adjusting for age, sex, and smoking status.

A New Biomarker for Cancer Immunotherapy

The companion study turned to oncology. Among 3,476 cancer patients, including 1,218 with non-small cell lung cancer treated with checkpoint inhibitors, those with higher thymic health scores were significantly more likely to respond to immunotherapy and survive longer. The pattern was clearest in patients who had not previously received chemotherapy, which can suppress immune function.

This finding addresses what oncologists call the "host factor" — the patient's own physiology as distinct from the tumor's genetics. "Part of the reason why we haven't really come up with a measurement of the host factor is because it is very complex, and we don't fully understand which are the relevant variables," said Wen Wee Ma, a gastrointestinal oncologist at Cleveland Clinic who was not involved in the studies. He called the results "pretty amazing."

The Thymus Link to Lifestyle

The studies also identified modifiable factors tied to thymic health. Smoking, obesity, being underweight, metabolic syndrome, and chronic inflammation all correlated with poorer thymic scores. This raises the prospect that protecting the thymus could become a tangible goal for preventive medicine — not just an abstract aspiration.

The research builds on a 2023 New England Journal of Medicine paper that found patients who had their thymus removed faced nearly three times the all-cause mortality risk and double the cancer risk compared to matched controls. Together, these findings paint a consistent picture: the thymus is far from expendable.

Not Everyone Is Convinced

Important caveats remain. The studies demonstrate correlation, not causation. María Mittelbrunn, an immunologist at the Spanish Research Council and visiting professor at Columbia University, noted that the thymus could be "acting as a proxy for overall physiological health" rather than directly determining outcomes. Patients with healthier thymuses also showed lower inflammation, suggesting the scans may capture a broader state of immune fitness.

Juan Carlos Zúñiga-Pflücker, a thymus researcher at the University of Toronto, described the findings as "exciting" and "clear evidence for the importance of the thymus in keeping us healthy," but cautioned that it remains unclear exactly which aspect of thymic activity is responsible.y drives the observed benefits.

What Comes Next

Several research teams are already exploring whether thymic decline can be slowed or reversed. Aerts has signalled that future work will examine interventions to restore thymic function. The observation that the thymus shrinks rapidly during pregnancy and then rebounds afterward suggests the organ retains regenerative capacity even in adulthood.

For India's medical community and the global diaspora, the implications extend to cancer care, where immunotherapy use is expanding rapidly, and to aging research more broadly. If thymic health scores prove clinically actionable, a routine CT scan could one day tell patients not just what ails them, but how well their immune system is equipped to protect them in the years ahead.
